name: Yucuna
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Yucuna (yucu1253) is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Robayo Romero 2018 (Forma y Función, open access, already on file), is directly about word prominence: an instrumental study showing that the Schauers' 'phonemic stress' marks track f0 rather than intensity, that words carry more than one prominence, and that Yukuna is better analysed as a two-tone language with lexically tone-specified roots and suffixes (pp.35, 39-44, 58-60). I also read the four other first-hand sources on file (Schauer & Schauer 1967 and 1978 stress analysis: phonemic, 1-3 stresses per word, intrinsic vs nonintrinsic stress shifting onto suffixes; Lemus Serrano 2020 PhD sec.1.2 and Lemus-Serrano et al. 2021 Glossa sec.2: restricted privative H-tone system, obligatory but not culminative) and newly fetched sources Schauer & Schauer 1972 'Fonología del yucuna' (SIL 18919, via a 2024 Wayback capture; All sources agree that prominence is lexical and positionally unpredictable; the modern sources code it as tone, not stress. Best statement: Lemus-Serrano et al. 2021 p.3. Not obtained: Lemus Serrano 2016 MA (stress analysis, not on HAL), Ramirez 2001 p.359, Schauer & Schauer 2000 (no PDF) — all low priority since superseded by the 2018-2021 work. only direct fetches were possible.

new_statements.quote: Yukuna’s word-prosodic system can be described as a restricted tonal system of the privative type, where H tone contrasts with the absence of tone. Such system corresponds to what is commonly labeled as ‘pitch accent’. However, we avoid the latter term, following the property-driven typological phonology approach (Hyman 2009). [...] When roots are produced without affixes, the following distributional rules apply: i) each root has at least one H syllable (e.g. *LLL), ii) each root has at most two H syllables (e.g. *HHH), iii) if there are two H tones, they are obligatorily adjacent (e.g. *HLH). [...] [p.5] The phonological sketch by Schauer & Schauer (1972: 71) explicitly mentions the phenomenon of shifting prosodic patterns caused by affixation, and provides an analysis of this phenomenon in terms of stress.
new_statements.citation: Lemus-Serrano, Magdalena, Marc Allassonnière-Tang & Dan Dediu. 2021. What conditions tone paradigms in Yukuna: Phonological and machine learning approaches. Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 6(1): 60, 1-22. doi:10.5334/gjgl.1276

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: (1) Quote check: extracted text of p.3 gives, word for word, 'Yukuna's word-prosodic system can be described as a restricted tonal system of the privative type, where H tone contrasts with the absence of tone. Such system corresponds to what is commonly labeled as 'pitch accent'. However, we avoid the latter term, following the property-driven typological phonology approach (Hyman 2009).' followed by the three distributional rules (*LLL, *HHH, *HLH) exactly as quoted; p.5 has verbatim 'The phonological sketch by Schauer & Schauer (1972: 71) explicitly mentions the phenomenon of shifting prosodic patterns caused by affixation, and provides an analysis of this phenomenon in terms of stress.'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No predictable word stress: word-level prominence is a lexically located H tone (privative H vs. zero, 'pitch-accent'-like restricted tone). Every root carries one underlying /H/ (spreads one syllable rightward) or /HL/ (non-spreading), bound to a lexically specified syllable or floating onto following toneless material; most affixes are toneless, so surface H position shifts under suffixation. The position of H within the root is not predictable from word edges or weight (attested root patterns 2σ HH/HL/LH, 3σ HHL/LHH/HLL/LLH/LHL). Earlier SIL descriptions (Schauer & Schauer 1967: 65-68; 1978: 10-13) described the same facts as phonemic (lexical) stress with 'intrinsic' vs 'nonintrinsic' stress and regular shifts: nonintrinsic stress on the final stem syllable of verbs shifting to the following suffix syllable, and on the first syllable of disyllabic nouns shifting to the possessive suffix.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Modern analysis: none (a second surface H results from /H/ spreading; HLH second H lowered by downdrift). Schauer & Schauer 1978: 11 speak of a primary accent (higher pitch and intensity, usually on the base) and a secondary accent occurring only on affixes; 1967: 66 'Yucuna appears to have a multiple stress system' with up to three stresses per word.
new_statements.exceptions: Purposive suffix /-tʃí/ (and /-ɾé/) carry their own H unlike other (toneless) affixes; some irregular paradigms remain unexplained (Glossa sec. 5). Schauer & Schauer 1967: 68 note intrinsic stress on verb affixes -la, -ra, -he; 1978: 12 rare accent shift across a word boundary.
new_statements.domain_note: Root/word-level lexical tone; Glossa data are verb paradigms (80 roots x ~30 affix combinations) recorded in non-final position in a frame sentence, Leticia 2017-18, validated with other speakers; Robayo Romero 2018 shows instrumentally that f0, not intensity or duration, is the correlate of the prominence the Schauers wrote as stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language, Yucuna/Yukuna (yucu1253, ISO ycn), spoken on the Mirití-Paraná (Amazonas, Colombia) and by migrants in Leticia; speakers include ethnic Matapí whose original language is lost (Schauer & Schauer 1967: 62). Self-designation kamejeya. No dialect split is reported. Note the analytical split: SIL sources (1967, 1972, 1978) = lexical/phonemic stress with morphological shifts; Robayo Romero 2018 and Lemus Serrano 2020/2021 = restricted privative tone (H vs zero), i.e. the same lexical prominence reanalysed as tone.

new_statements.quote: Yukuna's word-prosodic system can be described as a restricted tonal system of the privative type, where H tone contrasts with the absence of tone. Such system corresponds to what is commonly labeled as 'pitch accent'. However, we avoid the latter term, following the property-driven typological phonology approach (Hyman 2009). In addition to having a limited tonal inventory (H vs. absence of H), Yukuna also displays low tonal density, in terms of the number and distribution of surface H syllables. When roots are produced without affixes, the following distributional rules apply: i) each root has at least one H syllable (e.g. *LLL), ii) each root has at most two H syllables (e.g. *HHH), iii) if there are two H tones, they are obligatorily adjacent (e.g. *HLH).
new_statements.citation: Lemus-Serrano, Magdalena, Marc Allassonnière-Tang & Dan Dediu (2021). What conditions tone paradigms in Yukuna: phonological and machine learning approaches. Glossa 6(1): 60, 1-22. doi:10.5334/gjgl.1276
new_statements.locator: sec.2 'The phonology of Yukuna's tonal system', p.3 (PDF p.3)
new_statements.reading: Yukuna has no positional word stress. Word-level prominence is a lexically specified privative H tone (underlying /H/ spreading vs /HL/ non-spreading vs toneless syllables), obligatory (at least one H per word) but not strictly culminative (up to two adjacent H), with lexically unpredictable position and complex, partly irregular interaction with suffixes. This is the current consensus of the three first-hand modern sources (Robayo 2018 instrumental study, Lemus Serrano 2020 thesis, Lemus-Serrano et al. 2021); the older SIL analysis (Schauer & Schauer 1967/1972/1978) called the same phenomenon 'phonemic stress' with 'intrinsic' (lexically fixed, any stem syllable) vs 'nonintrinsic' (stem-final in verbs, initial in disyllabic nouns, shifting onto suffixes) types and 1-3 stresses per word. For catalog coding: lexical/unpredictable prominence (tone-accent), not a fixed-position stress system.

sources.quote: In Yukuna, pitch variations are lexically distinctive, that is to say, there are pairs of segmentally identical words that can be distinguished through their respective pitch patterns. Phonetically, there are three pitch levels at play: low, mid and high, whilst phonemically, only two levels are contrastive: low (L) and high (H). ... Yukuna's word prosodic system can be described as a 'restricted' tonal system, or what is commonly called a 'pitch accent' system. ... All roots are specified for tone, while most affixes are toneless. [pp.8-9]
sources.note: Ch. sketch sec. 1 (p. 5-6): 'the tonal system (previously analyzed as a stress system)'. Sec. 1.2 Prosody (pp. 8-9): pitch is lexically distinctive; two contrastive levels; restricted tonal system 'or what is commonly called a pitch accent system' (term avoided); two phonemic H tones /H/ spreading and /HL/ non-spreading, no phonemic L, toneless syllables default L; all roots specified for tone, most affixes toneless; table of attested root tone patterns (1σ H; 2σ HH, HL, LH; 3σ HHL, LHH, HLL, LLH, LHL; *LLL, *HHH, *HLH). No separate word stress is described.

sources.citation: Schauer, Stanley & Junia G. Schauer (1972). Fonología del yucuna. In Sistemas fonológicos de idiomas colombianos 1, 65-76. Lomalinda: ILV.
sources.quote: El acento es fonémico como se puede mostrar en las siguientes palabras: /virá/ 'él serrucha' /víra/ 'la sangre (de él)' ... Las polisílabas pueden tener de uno a tres acentos. Sinembargo, hasta ahora solo se ha encontrado una palabra con tres acentos. Cada sílaba acentuada tiene el mismo grado de intensidad y tono. /unká risápáláhe/ 'él no trabajará' [p.69] ... En los verbos, el acento extrínseco ocurre solo en sílabas finales de raíz. El traslado del acento es regularmente a la sílaba que sigue a la raíz. El acento intrínseco se puede presentar en cualquier sílaba de la raíz. [p.71]
sources.locator: sec.5 printed p.69 (PDF p.15); sec.6.6 printed pp.71-73 (PDF pp.17-19)
sources.note: Spanish version of the 1967 chapter (this is the edition Lemus-Serrano et al. 2021 cite as 'Schauer & Schauer 1972: 71'). Adds the sentence that every stressed syllable has the same degree of intensity and pitch (i.e. no culminative primary stress) — the observation Robayo 2018 uses to argue the system is tonal. sources.citation: Robayo Romero, Camilo Alberto. 2018. Introducción a la prosodia del verbo yukuna. Forma y Función 31(1): 33-63. doi:10.15446/fyf.v31n1.70442
sources.quote: Más de un acento primario por palabra contradice la definición de acento (Garde, 1968; Hyman, 2006), lo que invita a revisar los datos y a explorar otras interpretaciones. [p.35] ... En términos generales, se ha abierto una nueva perspectiva de análisis: entender la lengua yukuna como una lengua tonal con un sistema de dos tonos, alto y bajo. Tanto las raíces como los sufijos tienen en cada una de sus vocales una especificación de tono como parte de su identidad léxica [p.60]
sources.locator: Resumen p.33; Introducción p.35; Discusión pp.59-60
sources.note: Instrumental (Praat) study of inflected verbs in frame sentences with two speaker pairs from the Mirití-Paraná: tests Schauer & Schauer's (1978: 11-13) phonemic-stress claims; intensity peaks do not align with their accent marks and duration is independent of pitch; f0 contour is the relevant cue; proposes Yukuna is tonal (two levels, alto/bajo) rather than accentual, with root tone patterns and tonal polarity on the first post-root suffix. Notes that 'more than one primary accent per word contradicts the definition of stress'.

sources.citation: Schauer, Stanley & Junia G. Schauer (1978). Una gramática del yucuna. Artículos en Lingüística y Campos Afines 5: 1-52. Lomalinda: ILV.
sources.quote: El acento es fonémico, como se muestra por las palabras siguientes: /virá/ 'él asierra' /víra/ 'su sangre' /patáta/ 'trate (Ud.)' /pata'á/ 'robe (Ud.)'. Las palabras polisílabas pueden tener de uno a tres acentos ... Con relación a las palabras, el acento es de dos tipos: intrínseco y extrínseco. ... En los verbos el acento extrínseco aparece sólo en las sílabas al final de la base. Por lo general éste se traslada a la sílaba que sigue la base. El acento intrínseco puede aparecer en cualquier sílaba de la base. ... El acento primario (´), que lleva un grado más alto de tono e intensidad, usualmente aparece en la sílaba de la base, mientras que el acento secundario (,) ocurre sólo en los afijos. [pp.10-11]

sources.citation: Schauer, Stanley & Junia G. Schauer (1967). Yucuna phonemics. In V. G. Waterhouse (ed.), Phonemic Systems of Colombian Languages (SIL Publications in Linguistics 14), 61-71. Norman: SIL/Univ. of Oklahoma.
sources.quote: Stress is phonemic as shown by the following words: /rirá/ 'he saws' /rír a/ 'his blood' ... Stress is not limited to one syllable per word. Rather, Yucuna appears to have a multiple stress system [pp.65-66] ... In relation to words, stress appears to be of two types: intrinsic and nonintrinsic. ... Intrinsic stress in general is nonperturbable and may cause stress perturbation. Nonintrinsic stress is perturbable. ... In verbs nonintrinsic stress occurs only on final stem syllable. The shift of stress is regularly to the syllable following the stem. Intrinsic stress may occur on any stem syllable. ... In two-syllable nouns nonintrinsic stress falls on the first syllable. With such nouns there is shift of stress to the possessive suffix. [pp.67-68]
sources.note: Earliest first-hand description (fieldwork 1963-65): stress phonemic (minimal pairs), multiple stresses per word, two stress types (intrinsic = lexically fixed, any stem syllable; nonintrinsic = stem-final in verbs, initial in disyllabic nouns, shifting rightward onto suffixes). 'The full system has not yet been worked out.' Reanalyzed as tone by Robayo 2018 and Lemus Serrano 2020/2021.
